case_prompt: A 41-year-old man presented in May 2013 with a 20 × 18 cm area of cutaneous necrosis on the left thigh. He noted a 4 × 5 cm nodule at the same site in April without redness, pruritus, or pain, which progressed to necrosis over two weeks. He had no history of medication use, trauma, fever, or family history of thrombophilia. On admission, he reported mild right-sided chest pain and cough productive of bloody sputum but denied fever or dyspnea. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (36.59 × 10^9/L) with hypereosinophilia (21.15 × 10^9/L; 57.8%), thrombocytopenia (19 × 10^9/L), elevated liver enzymes (ALT 178 IU/L; AST 68 IU/L; GGT 329 IU/L), mildly increased procalcitonin (0.51 ng/mL), elevated fibrinogen (4.15 g/L), and a markedly increased D-dimer (82.20 mg/L FEU). The workup for allergic, parasitic, rheumatologic, and immunologic diseases was unremarkable. Chest CT revealed bilateral patchy pulmonary opacities and a small pleural effusion; abdominal ultrasound was normal. Skin biopsy of the necrotic lesion showed dermal necrosis and hemorrhage with perivascular lymphocytes, histiocytes, and eosinophils. Bone marrow aspiration demonstrated eosinophils comprising 27.5% of leukocytes.

selection.screen_reason: Marked hypereosinophilia with skin necrosis and lung infiltrates after a negative secondary-cause workup supports idiopathic HES.
